title: Four centuries to ChatGPT
dek: Modern AI is the confluence of ideas born centuries apart and for very different reasons: splitting wagers, computing orbits, sending messages over the telephone. Here they are in order, two winters included. Filter by chapter to follow the thread of each theory.

eras.title: The foundations
eras.text: Probability, calculus and linear algebra: tools created for gambling, physics and astronomy, which three centuries later would serve to learn from data.

eras.title: Computation and information are born
eras.text: Turing defines what computing is, Shannon what information is, and McCulloch and Pitts imagine neurons that compute.

eras.title: The first spring
eras.text: AI gets its name. Boundless optimism: perceptrons, programs that play checkers and chatbots that imitate a psychotherapist.

eras.title: The first winter
eras.text: The promises are not kept, funding is cut and neural networks fall out of favour after Minsky and Papert's book. Quietly, backpropagation is invented.

eras.title: Expert systems and connectionism
eras.text: Companies invest in systems built on hand-written rules. In parallel, neural networks are reborn with backpropagation.

eras.title: The second winter
eras.text: The Lisp machine market collapses and expert systems prove expensive and brittle. Theory, however, moves forward: universal approximation, vanishing gradients, support vectors.

eras.title: Statistical learning
eras.text: AI becomes probabilistic and data-driven. Methods with theoretical guarantees dominate, while neural networks wait for their moment: data and compute.

eras.title: Deep learning
eras.text: GPUs, large datasets and a few technical tricks: deep networks sweep vision, speech and games.

eras.label: 2017 – today
eras.title: Transformers and language models
eras.text: Attention replaces recurrence, scaling laws guide investment, and next-word prediction becomes general-purpose assistants.

events.title: Pascal and Fermat invent probability
events.text: A correspondence about how to split the stakes of an interrupted game founds the calculus of probability.

events.title: The chain rule
events.text: Leibniz differentiates composite functions in his notes. Three centuries later, backpropagation will be this rule applied systematically.

events.title: Law of large numbers
events.text: Ars Conjectandi is published posthumously: the observed frequency converges to the true probability.

events.title: Bayes' theorem
events.text: Price publishes Bayes's posthumous essay on reasoning from effects back to causes.

events.title: Least squares
events.text: Legendre publishes the method for fitting the orbits of comets. Gauss had used it to recover the dwarf planet Ceres in 1801. It is the first “loss function”.

events.title: Spaces of any dimension
events.text: Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre introduces vector spaces with any number of dimensions.

events.title: Gradient descent
events.text: To solve astronomical equations, Cauchy proposes walking down step by step in the direction of steepest slope.

events.title: The theory of matrices
events.text: Cayley defines the matrix product and treats matrices as algebraic objects in their own right.

events.title: Maximum likelihood
events.text: Fisher formalizes the principle of choosing the parameters that make the data most probable: the objective every LLM is trained with.

events.title: The decision problem
events.text: Is there a mechanical procedure that decides whether any logical statement can be proved?

events.title: The incompleteness theorems
events.text: Every sufficiently powerful consistent formal system contains truths it cannot prove.

events.title: The Turing machine
events.text: Turing defines computation with a tape and a table of rules, describes the universal machine and proves that the halting problem is undecidable.

events.title: The logical neuron
events.text: The first mathematical model of a network of neurons: thresholds that compute logical functions.

events.title: The stored-program computer
events.text: The EDVAC report describes the architecture in which program and data share memory.

events.title: A mathematical theory of communication
events.text: Shannon defines entropy, proves the limits of compression and generates text with $n$-gram models.

events.title: Hebb's rule
events.text: “Neurons that fire together wire together”: the first hypothesis about how a network learns.

events.title: The imitation game
events.text: “Computing Machinery and Intelligence” proposes the Turing test and suggests building machines that learn like a child.

events.title: Stochastic approximation
events.text: You can optimize with noisy estimates of the gradient if the learning rate decreases appropriately.

events.title: The Kullback–Leibler divergence
events.text: A measure of distance between distributions that reappears in training and in RLHF.

events.title: Huffman codes
events.text: A simple algorithm builds the optimal prefix-free code for a given distribution.

events.title: “Artificial intelligence” is born
events.who: John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, Claude Shannon
events.text: The Dartmouth summer workshop gives the field its name. The proposal (1955) estimated that a select group could make “a significant advance” in two months.

events.title: The perceptron
events.text: An artificial neuron with a learning rule. The following year the Mark I Perceptron is unveiled.

events.title: Dynamic programming
events.text: The Bellman equation founds sequential decision-making, the basis of reinforcement learning.

events.title: The maximum entropy principle
events.text: The least committed distribution compatible with what we know is exponential: the softmax with temperature.

events.title: “Machine learning”
events.text: A checkers program that improves by playing against itself popularizes the term machine learning.

events.title: Perceptron convergence
events.text: If the data are separable with margin $\gamma$, the perceptron makes at most $(R/\gamma)^2$ mistakes.

events.title: The heavy ball
events.text: The momentum method speeds up gradient descent in elongated valleys.

events.title: ELIZA
events.text: A program of simple rules that imitates a psychotherapist. Many users credit it with real understanding, to its author's alarm.

events.title: Perceptrons
events.text: A rigorous analysis of the limitations of the single-layer perceptron, with XOR as the famous example.

events.title: Reverse-mode automatic differentiation
events.text: A Finnish master's thesis describes the algorithm we now call backpropagation.

events.title: The VC dimension
events.text: A combinatorial measure of the capacity of a class of models that determines when generalization is possible.

events.title: The Lighthill report
events.text: A highly critical report for the British government triggers cuts in AI research funding.

events.title: Backpropagation for neural networks
events.text: Werbos proposes in his thesis training multi-layer networks with reverse-mode differentiation. It goes almost unnoticed.

events.title: The Neocognitron
events.text: A hierarchical network inspired by the visual cortex: a forerunner of convolutional networks.

events.title: Hopfield networks
events.text: A recurrent network that works as an associative memory, analysed with tools from statistical physics.

events.title: The accelerated method
events.text: A first-order method with error $O(1/k^2)$, the best possible for smooth convex functions.

events.title: PAC learning
events.text: “A Theory of the Learnable” gives a formal definition of learning: probably approximately correct.

events.title: The Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma
events.text: Many points fit in few dimensions without distorting their distances: the geometry that embeddings exploit.

events.title: Backpropagation goes mainstream
events.who: David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, Ronald Williams
events.text: A paper in Nature shows that multi-layer networks learn useful internal representations.

events.title: The Lisp machine market collapses
events.text: General-purpose computers catch up with machines specialized for AI and drag the expert-systems industry down with them.

events.title: Universal approximation
events.who: George Cybenko; Kurt Hornik, Maxwell Stinchcombe, Halbert White
events.text: A single hidden layer is enough to approximate any continuous function.

events.title: Convolutional networks read ZIP codes
events.text: A network trained with backpropagation reads handwritten digits for the US Postal Service.

events.title: Simple recurrent networks
events.text: A network with memory of its own state discovers structure in sequences of words.

events.title: The vanishing gradient
events.text: A diploma thesis explains why deep and recurrent networks fail to learn long-range dependencies.

events.title: Support vector machines
events.who: Bernhard Boser, Isabelle Guyon, Vladimir Vapnik
events.text: Maximum-margin classifiers with theoretical guarantees: the star method of the following decade.

events.title: TD-Gammon
events.text: A neural network trained by reinforcement, playing against itself, reaches the level of the best backgammon players.

events.title: Byte Pair Encoding
events.text: A compression algorithm that, twenty years later, will be used to cut text into tokens.

events.title: No free lunch
events.text: No learning algorithm beats another when averaged over all problems: an inductive bias is needed.

events.title: LSTM
events.text: The gates of long short-term memory let recurrent networks remember for hundreds of steps.

events.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
events.text: Massive search and hand-designed evaluation, with no deep learning: the other tradition of AI.

events.title: A neural language model
events.text: Word embeddings learned together with a network that predicts the next word.

events.title: Deep belief networks
events.who: Geoffrey Hinton, Simon Osindero, Yee-Whye Teh
events.text: Layer-by-layer pretraining revives interest in deep networks.

events.title: ImageNet
events.text: A database of millions of labelled images, and a yearly competition that will measure progress in vision.

events.title: AlexNet
events.who: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Geoffrey Hinton
events.text: A convolutional network trained on GPUs wins ImageNet with a top-5 error of 15.3%, ten points below the runner-up.

events.title: word2vec
events.text: Embeddings trained at scale in which semantic relations become directions: king − man + woman ≈ queen.

events.title: Attention for translation
events.who: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio
events.text: The decoder learns to focus on the relevant words of the input sentence.

events.title: Adam
events.text: An optimizer with momentum and an adaptive learning rate for each parameter.

events.title: Residual networks
events.text: Residual connections make it possible to train networks of over a hundred layers without the gradient vanishing.

events.title: AlphaGo beats Lee Sedol
events.text: Deep networks, search and reinforcement learning defeat the champion at the game of Go, a decade earlier than expected.

events.title: “Attention Is All You Need”
events.who: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin
events.text: The Transformer drops recurrence: only attention, in parallel.

events.title: Reinforcement from human preferences
events.text: A reward model trained on human comparisons guides reinforcement learning.

events.title: Rethinking generalization
events.text: Networks memorize random labels perfectly: classical bounds do not explain their success.

events.title: GPT and BERT
events.text: Pretraining a Transformer on unlabelled text and then fine-tuning it breaks records on almost every language task.

events.title: GPT-2 and double descent
events.text: A 1.5-billion-parameter model writes surprisingly coherent text; in parallel, overparameterized models are shown to improve again.

events.title: Scaling laws and GPT-3
events.who: Jared Kaplan and colleagues; Tom Brown and colleagues
events.text: Loss falls as a power law. GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, learns new tasks from a few examples in the prompt itself.

events.title: LoRA
events.text: Adapting a huge model by training only low-rank corrections.

events.title: Chinchilla
events.text: With fixed compute, parameters and data should grow together: about 20 tokens per parameter.

events.title: ChatGPT
events.text: On 30 November a model fine-tuned with RLHF opens to the public. A million users in five days.

events.title: Direct preference optimization
events.text: The exact solution of the KL-regularized objective makes it possible to align models without explicit reinforcement learning.

events.title: Nobel prizes for neural networks
events.who: John Hopfield, Geoffrey Hinton; Demis Hassabis, John Jumper, David Baker
events.text: The Nobel Prize in Physics rewards the foundations of artificial neural networks, and the Chemistry prize protein structure prediction with AlphaFold (together with protein design).

events.title: Calibrated models hallucinate
events.text: A statistical lower bound on the hallucination rate of calibrated language models.

events.title: The 5-state busy beaver is settled
events.text: A formally verified proof establishes that the 5-state machine that takes longest to halt runs for 47,176,870 steps.

events.title: Reasoning models
events.text: Models trained with reinforcement on verifiable problems that “think” before answering, trading compute at answer time for accuracy.
